CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
### The Interval

At first, you would mistake it for a surveying error.

A ridge on the horizon appears slightly nearer than it should. A falling shard of mineral takes too long to reach the ground. Between two flashes of lightning, your instruments record a third flash that your eyes never saw.

These discrepancies move together. They are one creature.

The Interval lives on a planet without a stable surface. Under immense atmospheric pressure, broad plains of translucent mineral continually change phase: solid becoming liquid, liquid becoming something with the rigidity of glass and the internal motion of a storm. Mountains form in an afternoon and remain upright for centuries after their foundations have flowed away.

Within this material, the Interval exists as a mobile arrangement of defects.

It is not made *of* the mineral, any more than a knot is made of a particular length of rope. Matter passes through it and is reorganized. Its identity resides in the relationships between thousands of microscopic boundaries: where one crystalline orientation becomes another, where pressure changes direction, where an electrical charge cannot quite escape.

No atom stays part of it for long.

### Its body

A mature Interval occupies roughly a cubic kilometer, although most of that volume contains nothing belonging to it. Its active structure consists of disconnected sheets, threads, and points. Some are closer to one another structurally than they are spatially: disturbing a point near the surface may immediately alter a sheet deep underground while leaving everything between them untouched.

It has no inside. Nor does it have a consistent number of parts.

When conditions are favorable, it becomes elaborate, extending delicate faults through the surrounding terrain. During violent weather, it simplifies into a handful of stubborn relationships preserved in dense stone.

Seen with the right instruments, it resembles a diagram constantly revising what its lines mean.

### How it lives

The Interval feeds on delayed change.

Its planet’s minerals frequently remain poised between states. A plain may be ready to crystallize but lack the tiny disturbance needed to begin. The Interval introduces that disturbance selectively, guiding the released energy through its own network.

Behind a feeding Interval, the landscape becomes unnaturally settled. Glass clears. Buried tensions vanish. Storms lose their electrical charge.

Ahead of it, the ground sometimes shivers in anticipation.

Its waste is not a substance but a condition: matter from which useful possibilities have been exhausted. An old feeding ground can remain sterile to its kind for thousands of years, despite looking chemically identical to healthy terrain.

### What it perceives

It does not perceive objects.

Its nearest equivalent to sight is an awareness of **what could happen next**.

A mountain is not a shape but a family of potential collapses. A storm is a branching arrangement of possible discharges. Another Interval is recognizable because certain changes become less available while others become suspiciously easy.

Its perceptual world is rich in almost-events.

Human movement would be difficult for it to distinguish from weather. A human-made machine, however, might be startlingly conspicuous: an improbable system that repeatedly forces the same outcome.

### How it reproduces

Two Intervals reproduce by making a place neither can inhabit.

They overlap their outer structures and gradually constrain a volume of mineral until it can sustain a new, incompatible arrangement. For a time, the developing offspring exists only as pressure on its parents: both must continually change to accommodate something not yet present.

Then the new arrangement stabilizes.

The parents withdraw, permanently altered. The offspring inherits neither parent’s shape, but some of their preferences—which instabilities it seeks, which patterns it can survive, which transformations it finds intolerable.

Occasionally, one parent emerges as three individuals. Occasionally, two leave as one. Individuality is a temporary property of the process.

### Encounter

You could stand within an Interval without knowing it.

Your equipment would develop correlated faults. A warm battery would cool while a disconnected wire began to hum. Beneath your boots, fractures would appear in patterns that almost repeated.

If it noticed you, it might investigate by preventing small things from happening.

A switch would fail to close. A bead of condensation would refuse to fall.

Then, perhaps, every loose stone around you would turn over at once.

Not a greeting. Not a threat.

It would be trying to determine which of your possibilities were you.

A pale region advances through a black plain, perhaps half a kilometer across. Nothing walks. Nothing flows. The surface does not rise or fall. The planet has no exposed water and almost no distinction between weather and geology. Beneath an atmosphere dense enough to crush an Earth submarine, heat and tidal pressure continually force molten salts through a porous mineral crust. Electrical currents wander through the ground. Life arose within those transitions.

The minerals are its temporary medium, not its permanent flesh.

### What its body is

A Vey consists of thousands of linked boundaries between different states of crystalline matter. Along these boundaries, ions travel readily in one direction and poorly in another. Together, they form a sprawling electrical and chemical circuit.

That circuit controls the conditions that keep the boundaries in existence.

It is a body that continually builds the circumstances necessary to remain a body.

Individual pieces of mineral enter its organization, participate for a while, and leave again unchanged or subtly altered. Over the course of a few days, almost none of its original material remains.

Its shape is stranger still. A Vey might occupy a broad sheet underground, six thin columns nearer the surface, and a scatter of apparently isolated patches several meters away. These parts communicate through currents passing across the intervening rock.

The gaps are as essential as the occupied regions. Fill one with an especially conductive substance, and you might injure it by connecting things that must remain separate.

A specimen dug out of the ground would be nothing but hot, unremarkable stones. Capturing one would require preserving a volume of landscape, its pressure gradients, and its continuing supply of chemical disequilibrium.

### How it feeds and moves

The Vey feeds where tidal pumping brings chemically incompatible salts close together.

It selectively opens pathways between them, allowing reactions to occur through its own circuit. Some of the released energy maintains its organization; some drives changes in the neighboring minerals.

Movement is therefore a controlled succession of recruitment and release. It establishes part of its pattern ahead of itself, then lets the trailing part dissolve.

It does not crawl across the ground. **It persuades the ground ahead to become it.**

There is no fixed front. It can advance in several directions, abandon most of them, or stretch around an obstacle while keeping its most important processes elsewhere.

Under favorable conditions, it may remain in one place for centuries, moving internally without changing its outline.

### What it perceives

A Vey has no eyes, ears, or central vantage point.

Its surroundings alter the currents passing through it. A distant fracture changes the resistance of one route. An approaching pressure wave shifts the timing of hundreds of reactions. A buried deposit announces itself as a faint, persistent bias in ion movement.

Its perceptual world would not resemble a picture.

Even that is only an analogy.

Its fastest responses take seconds. Others require several local years. It can react to an approaching geological disturbance while remaining effectively unaware of a small object rapidly crossing its surface.

A human tapping on the ground above it would not be knocking on its door. They would be producing an irrelevant flicker in one tiny portion of its existence.

### Memory and reproduction

Past activity leaves microscopic defects in the crystals it has used. When currents revisit those defects, they favor certain routes over others.

Some memories travel with the creature because it copies these biases into newly recruited material. Others remain embedded in abandoned ground.

Returning to an old location can therefore restore information the Vey no longer carries.

Reproduction occurs when it constructs a second, partly independent circuit around a new energy source. For a time, the two share control pathways. Then the links weaken.

What passes to the offspring is not a miniature body, but an arrangement of timing relationships and preferred transformations: instructions expressed as physical tendencies.

Copying is imperfect. Some offspring maintain themselves better than others. Over immense spans of time, their lineages evolve.

If you stood above a Vey during a reproductive separation, you might see pale geometric regions appear across the plain. Some would brighten, vanish, and recur farther away. The ground would make no sound audible to you.

For weeks, two patterns would alternately stabilize and disrupt each other.

Then, one evening, the interference would stop.

One pale region would remain. The other would slowly extend beneath a ridge.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
### The Unfinished

On the planet Orthe, the distinction between geology and biology was discovered to be a mistake.

Orthe is a massive, slowly rotating world with an atmosphere so dense that its lowest layers behave more like hot solvent than air. Beneath its surface lies a mantle of translucent minerals. Pressure makes these minerals change structure: their atoms rearrange, their electrical properties shift, and some release energy when they pass from one crystalline state into another.

Something lives in those transitions.

Human explorers call it **the Unfinished**, because no observation has ever caught it existing as a complete object.

### What it looks like

A specimen occupies perhaps thirty cubic kilometers of rock, but almost none of that rock is properly its body.

Its body is a particular arrangement of *changes*: a branching sequence of crystal transformations, electrical discharges, and migrating pressure fronts. Material enters and leaves the arrangement continuously. The creature remains itself in roughly the way a melody remains itself when played on a different instrument—except that this melody builds its own instrument as it goes.

If you could stand inside the mantle without being crushed, you would see faint planes of violet light appearing in the stone. Some would be broad enough to stretch beyond sight; others would be thinner than a human hair. They would brighten, divide, and vanish.

Occasionally, a dark volume would drift through the luminous planes. This would not be a shadow. It would be a region in which the creature had temporarily suppressed the mineral’s ability to transmit light.

There would be no central mass to point to. Two illuminated patches a kilometer apart might belong to the same individual, while a third patch between them belonged to something else.

Its most distinctive feature would be a recurring imperfection: every branching pattern would stop just short of closing. Those tiny gaps keep the system active. A perfectly completed pattern would settle into equilibrium.

For this creature, symmetry is a kind of death.

### How it eats

The Unfinished consumes **stored strain**.

Orthe’s immense tides slowly deform its interior. Certain minerals become trapped in unstable configurations, holding energy like compressed springs. The creature guides a transformation through them, releasing that energy in carefully staggered increments.

Some becomes heat. Some drives electrical currents. Some is used to prepare neighboring stone so that the creature’s pattern can continue into it.

After feeding, it leaves behind broad, mechanically relaxed regions that other individuals cannot use until the tides strain them again. From orbit, these feeding grounds appear as subtle changes in the timing of planetary tremors.

It can starve in a mountain of chemically suitable material if that material has become too comfortable.

### What it perceives

It has no eyes, ears, skin, or equivalent organs.

Every part of its active pattern is affected by the rock around it. A fracture a hundred kilometers away alters the arrival time of a pressure wave. A nearby individual changes electrical resistance along a shared mineral seam. The movement of a moon overhead gradually changes which directions are easiest to grow into.

Its perceptual world is therefore made of **possibilities of movement and transformation**.

Where we might perceive a red cliff, it might perceive something closer to:

*An easy continuation, becoming difficult; a delayed release; a region that will resist after the next tide.*

Even this translation is misleading. Those are not separate observations followed by a decision. To perceive a possibility is already to begin extending into it.

### How it thinks

Its memory consists of changes it has made to its surroundings.

A mineral pathway used once becomes easier—or sometimes harder—to use again. The creature’s history is etched into the physical conditions governing its next action. Old feeding grounds, abandoned branches, and healed fractures participate in its thought long after its active body has moved away.

Consequently, removing an Unfinished from its territory would not simply displace it. It would amputate much of its memory.

A decision can take several local years. Yet some of the electrical events composing that decision last less than a microsecond. It has no single natural speed of life.

When confronted by an obstacle, it may send dozens of tentative continuations around and through it. Most fail. Their failures alter the stone, informing the surviving pathways.

It thinks by partially becoming things it ultimately does not become.

### How it reproduces

There is no birth event.

Sometimes a large individual develops two regions whose internal activity becomes increasingly independent. For centuries, they exchange energy and complete one another’s patterns. Eventually, each can persist without the other.

Whether there are now two creatures is not always a meaningful question.

The process can also reverse. Two individuals meeting in compatible rock may interlace so thoroughly that neither survives as a separate identity, although almost all their memories remain accessible to the resulting organism.

Reproduction, conversation, feeding, and healing share much of the same machinery.

### What meeting one would be like

The explorers’ first contact attempt involved sending rhythmic vibrations into the mantle.

For seventeen years, nothing happened.

Then the mineral beneath their transmitter rearranged itself into a structure that returned each signal slightly altered. Researchers initially interpreted this as an answer.

It was closer to a splint.

The Unfinished had understood the repetitive mechanical disturbance as a damaged process struggling to maintain itself. It was trying to help the transmitter become stable.

Its first act toward humanity was neither curiosity nor hostility. It had encountered something persistently unfinished and supplied the missing conditions.

When the researchers switched the transmitter off, the creature spent the next forty years trying to revive it.

The creature is the relationship between these appearances.

The deep planet continuously supplies heat. The upper layers continuously lose it. Between them lie reservoirs of ice trapped in unstable states.

An Unfinished feeds by persuading those reservoirs to settle.

Its passing leaves behind more stable crystal and releases energy, some of which sustains the next stages of its body. It does not consume matter; it consumes the availability of change.

A well-fed individual has many alternative routes through which its sequence can continue. A starving one becomes increasingly exact. Each event must occur in precisely the right place, at precisely the right moment.

Near death, it becomes exquisitely orderly.

Its world contains no visible objects.

It senses these through faint test pulses, most too weak to trigger anything. Returning distortions reveal the surrounding lattice’s readiness to change.

A human might perceive a wall. An Unfinished perceives a thousand potential continuations, all ending.

Another creature is recognizable not by shape but by a peculiar pattern of unavailable possibilities. Regions that ought to respond do not, because they have already been incorporated into someone else’s sequence.

Some transformations leave tiny defects in the lattice. When the creature’s cycle returns through that region, those defects alter its timing.

Its remains are unfinished bodily processes scattered through the ice.

Another creature may eventually incorporate one of them, acquiring both a useful route and the lattice defects that shaped it. Something resembling an ancient avoidance or preference can thus reappear in a creature that never experienced its cause.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
On the planet Vey, the ground is a hot, translucent mineral under pressures that would crush a submarine. It slowly changes phase as the planet’s three moons pull it into different shapes. There is no clear boundary between land and atmosphere: the mineral softens upward into a dense metallic mist.

Within this ground lives a creature we might call **the Unfastening**.

The name is misleading. It is not a thing that pulls other things apart. It is a particular way in which the world fails to stay together.

### Its body

The Unfastening consists of thousands of thin discontinuities in the mineral: surfaces where the atomic structure on one side does not quite agree with the structure on the other.

These surfaces curve, intersect, and slip through one another without opening into cracks. Together they form a moving three-dimensional pattern roughly the size of a cathedral, although size is not a reliable measure of the creature. Sometimes the same individual spreads across several kilometers; sometimes it concentrates into a volume smaller than a cupboard.

It contains no permanent substance. The mineral passes through its pattern as water passes through a whirlpool.

Nor does it have a definite inside or outside. A particular patch of ground can belong to the creature in one physical respect and to the surrounding planet in another. Two Unfastenings can occupy the same location without either encompassing the other.

If you could survive beside one and illuminate it, you would see nested sheets of faint iridescence suspended in the rock. Some would seem to intersect impossibly. As you moved your head, sections would disappear—not because they had become hidden, but because their optical properties no longer distinguished them from their surroundings.

Occasionally, a pale geometric flash would travel through the whole arrangement.

That would be closer to a heartbeat than anything else you could observe, though it might happen once in a second or not at all for a month.

### How it lives

The moons continually strain Vey’s crust. Much of that strain remains trapped in the mineral, like energy in a bent spring.

The Unfastening releases it selectively.

By rearranging its discontinuities, it encourages tiny regions of the ground to shift into more stable configurations. Some of the liberated energy maintains its intricate structure; the rest escapes as heat and vibration.

Its food is therefore neither matter nor light, but **unresolved mechanical tension**.

A well-fed region looks almost exactly like an exhausted one. The difference is in how much change remains possible there.

The creature moves by forming new discontinuities ahead of itself and allowing old ones to disappear behind it. No part pushes against the ground. Its movement is the propagation of a self-maintaining condition.

When threatened by a sudden fracture, it can abandon most of its extent and persist in a handful of deeply buried intersections. Recovering afterward may take centuries.

### What it perceives

The Unfastening has no eyes, ears, or central place where sensations arrive.

Every part of its structure responds to pressure, temperature, electrical charge, and the orientation of the surrounding crystal. A disturbance changes the pattern; the changed pattern alters which subsequent disturbances can pass through it.

Its experience, if it has one, might be less like seeing a landscape than inhabiting an enormous, continuously revised statement about what the landscape is capable of doing.

A mountain above it is not primarily a shape. It is a distribution of possible failures.

Another creature is not primarily an object. It is a recognizable influence on those possibilities.

Events at widely separated points can reach it together through fast vibrations, while nearby events arrive much later through slow deformation. Consequently, distance and sequence would not organize its world as neatly as they organize ours.

It might perceive a distant moonrise and a nearby slipping crystal as parts of a single occurrence.

### Memory and reproduction

Its memories are persistent changes in the way its surfaces intersect. An encounter leaves behind a geometry that makes some future responses easier and others harder.

Memory therefore has a physical cost. Too much retained experience makes the creature inflexible. Eventually, it must erase portions of itself to remain alive.

Reproduction happens during these erasures.

Sometimes a discarded configuration does not collapse. It catches enough strain from the surrounding mineral to sustain itself and begins extending its own surfaces.

The offspring inherits a fragment of the parent’s history rather than a miniature version of its body. One might begin with the structural memory of a catastrophe it never experienced. Another might inherit only the pattern associated with an unusually rich feeding ground.

There is no fixed number of parents. A viable new Unfastening can emerge where the abandoned memories of several individuals intersect.

### An encounter

Imagine lowering a pressure-proof instrument into Vey’s crust.

At first, it records random tremors.

Then the tremors begin arriving in intervals that match the instrument’s sampling cycle. You change the cycle. After several hours, the tremors change too.

The Unfastening has detected a small, remarkably regular source of disturbance. It grows around the probe, testing how the unfamiliar object redistributes stress. Your instruments register a succession of delicate compressions, each from a different direction.

Then the signals stop.

The probe still works. The creature is still there. But it has rearranged the mineral around your machine so precisely that the probe’s movements no longer produce detectable vibrations beyond a few centimeters.

Perhaps it has protected itself from an irritation. Perhaps it has stored the machine as a stable feature of its surroundings.

You could remain there for years, transmitting greetings into the perfectly fitted silence, without knowing which.

### The Unhappening

On a planet with no exposed surface, beneath an atmosphere thousands of kilometers deep, there is a mantle of hot, transparent ice. Pressure keeps it solid despite temperatures that would melt lead. Metallic salts run through it in branching seams, carrying electrical disturbances from the planet’s restless interior.

Something lives in the disturbances.

It is not made of the ice, or the salts, or any particular collection of atoms. It is a self-maintaining pattern of interruptions: a precise arrangement of places where electrical pulses arrive late.

We might call it an **Unhappening**.

### Its body

An Unhappening has no continuous outline. One individual might occupy nine pinprick regions scattered through a cubic kilometer of ice, plus a thin sheet several kilometers away. Between these regions lies ordinary, unoccupied material.

What makes them one creature is their timing.

Each region delays passing electrical pulses by a particular amount. Those delayed pulses reach other regions and help maintain their delays. Together, they form a closed, self-correcting circuit of causes. Remove one region, and the others adjust. Separate them too far, and the creature loses coherence.

Matter passes through its organization without being consumed. When it moves, it establishes new delays ahead of itself and releases old ones behind. It could cross a continent without carrying a single atom along.

Its size is therefore a misleading measurement. A healthy adult is better described as being **forty-three milliseconds deep**.

### What it looks like

To human eyes, most of it would be invisible.

But its activity slightly alters the crystalline structure around it. Shine a light through the inhabited ice, and you would see scattered patches of color that do not quite agree about where the light is coming from. Move your head, and one patch might turn violet while another appears to move backward.

At the center of a particularly active region, reflections would linger for a fraction of a second after the light was switched off.

These are not signals or decorations. They are incidental, like the sound your stomach makes.

A dying Unhappening would be briefly beautiful: all its delays collapsing into synchronization, producing a flash throughout widely separated portions of the ice. What looked like a constellation would turn out to have been one animal.

### How it eats

The planet’s interior sends up irregular electrical surges. The Unhappening feeds on the difference between their disorderly arrival and the orderly rhythm it imposes.

At each occupied region, it diverts a tiny fraction of a surge’s energy into rearranging charged defects in the ice. Those defects maintain the delays that constitute its body.

Its waste is heat and excessively regular electrical pulses.

A crowded habitat can consequently become uninhabitable: generations of Unhappenings gradually smooth the electrical turbulence on which they depend. Their equivalent of famine is a world that has become too predictable.

During scarcity, an individual stretches its timing. Processes that once took milliseconds take minutes, then years. A starving creature can persist as a set of almost imperceptible hesitations in the planet’s electrical weather.

### What it perceives

It has no privileged viewpoint—no place corresponding to a head.

Its sensations consist of relationships among events. It experiences distance as the difficulty of making two disturbances coincide. A physically nearby region behind an insulating seam is “far away”; a region hundreds of kilometers down a conductive channel is “close.”

It cannot see an object sitting motionless beside it. But it can sense the arrival of a pressure wave, the development of a fracture, or the changing electrical influence of another creature.

Its nearest equivalent to fear is discovering that its different parts can no longer agree on the order in which things happened.

Its nearest equivalent to pleasure is a complicated disturbance that it can absorb without losing itself.

### Its memory

An Unhappening remembers by retaining additional possible routes through its circuit.

An old individual contains many arrangements it is not currently using. If conditions change, it can reestablish a former configuration. Memory is less like an image of the past than a collection of bodies it knows how to become.

Some experiences permanently alter which configurations remain possible.

It does not remember an injury.

It remembers how to exist around the missing region.

### How it reproduces

Occasionally, an individual develops two incompatible but equally stable rhythms. Rather than choosing one, it maintains both until each becomes capable of supporting itself.

The offspring initially overlap completely.

Then they begin to disagree. One recruits a new region; the other releases an old one. Eventually, two creatures occupy different circuits.

There is no clear moment of birth, and no meaningful way to identify which is the parent.

Two individuals can also meet and exchange so many timing relationships that three depart—or one. This is neither mating nor eating, though it serves some purposes of both.

### What encountering one would mean

A drilling probe would introduce vibrations, heat, and unfamiliar electrical rhythms. An Unhappening might gather around these disturbances, not out of curiosity as we understand it, but because incorporating unfamiliar patterns is part of how it grows.

It might learn to anticipate the probe’s instruments. It might begin returning pulses.

The researchers could mistake this for communication.

The creature, meanwhile, might be making an equally profound mistake: slowly incorporating the probe into itself, trying to keep its strange new region alive.

When the humans finally switched their equipment off, it would spend years attempting to restore them.

CREATURE DESCRIPTION:
### The Interval

From orbit, its planet appears smooth and black. There are no oceans, clouds, or visible continents. A rigid mineral crust covers a deep mantle of hot crystalline matter, squeezed so tightly that electrical charge moves through it like water through a sponge.

The creature lives inside that mantle.

It is not made of the crystal. It is made of the disagreements between crystals.

Where neighboring mineral structures fail to align, narrow boundaries form. Most are inert. But one particular arrangement of boundaries can sustain itself: it redirects pressure, gathers electrical potential, and continually persuades the surrounding rock to preserve the mismatch.

That arrangement is the creature. We might call it an **Interval**.

### What it looks like

An Interval has no surface separating an inside from an outside. A typical adult occupies several cubic kilometers, but almost all that volume is ordinary planetary material. Its actual structure consists of branching flaws, some narrower than an atom, others broad enough to swallow a building.

If you could see through the mantle, it would resemble an immense, unfinished diagram: sheets intersecting at impossible-looking angles, loops that almost close, delicate forks interrupted by gaps.

Those gaps are essential organs.

A perfectly connected Interval would die. Its life depends on keeping certain parts of itself just out of contact, allowing differences in charge and strain to accumulate across them.

Its shape changes continuously. A vast section may vanish while another appears a kilometer away. Nothing travels between the two locations except a rearrangement of stresses. The creature moves somewhat as a crease moves across fabric, although its “fabric” is an entire geological layer.

It has no preferred size. Under favorable conditions, an individual can spread until different regions of its body experience measurably different gravity.

### How it feeds

It eats impending events.

More precisely, it feeds on rock that is close to changing state: a crystal about to buckle, a fault about to slip, a mineral about to acquire a new structure under pressure.

The Interval threads itself around that unstable region and delays the change. During the delay, it draws energy from the accumulating imbalance. Eventually, it permits the transformation in a carefully staged sequence, harvesting the release without allowing it to tear its own structure apart.

A feeding Interval leaves behind unusually orderly rock.

That is its waste: equilibrium.

An old feeding ground is a place where almost nothing interesting can happen. The creature must eventually move on, leaving a flawless, exhausted volume behind it.

### How it perceives

Light never reaches it. Sound, as a distinct category, means nothing to it; pressure is both the medium of its body and the substance of its awareness.

It senses **possibilities**.

Every surrounding crystal has several ways it could respond to a disturbance. The Interval detects these alternatives by sending tiny stresses outward and measuring the resistance that returns.

Its world is therefore not a collection of objects in locations. It is a landscape of things that might happen.

A nearby mineral deposit may be imperceptible if it is stable. A distant fault may dominate the creature’s awareness because it has a thousand possible futures, several of which threaten the Interval.

What we would call distance matters less to it than how strongly one event can alter another.

### How it remembers

It has no central processor. Memory is stored in transformations it has made slightly easier or harder.

After surviving a violent mantle shift, it retains minute structural biases that steer future disturbances away from similar outcomes. Remembering is not the retrieval of a record. It is finding that certain futures have become more accessible than others.

Some memories outlive the individual.

When an Interval abandons a region, another can occupy the remaining defects and acquire those tendencies. There is no clear distinction between inheriting a memory, learning something, and encountering an ancient wound in the landscape.

### How it reproduces

An Interval reproduces when it becomes unable to remain one creature.

As it grows, distant regions develop incompatible requirements. One portion needs a fault to open; another needs that same fault to stay sealed. For centuries, the whole organism may maintain elaborate compromises.

Eventually, a compromise fails.

The structure reorganizes into two independent patterns, each sustaining a different solution. Both inherit much of the original’s memory. Neither is the parent, exactly, and neither is the child.

Sometimes they remain interwoven, occupying the same volume while no longer constituting the same being.

### What an encounter would be like

A human drilling expedition would probably discover it as an engineering anomaly.

Boreholes would keep closing. Instruments would register coordinated stress changes far beyond the drill site. A supposedly dangerous fault would become inexplicably quiet.

The Interval would not initially distinguish the expedition from a novel mineral process. It might spend decades testing the machinery with gentle deformations.

Its first unmistakable communication would not be a sound or symbol.

It would arrange the surrounding rock so that, whenever the humans stopped drilling, a chamber opened safely below them.

Whenever they resumed, the chamber closed.

Whether this meant *come closer*, *stop hurting me*, or *please continue feeding me* would take a very long time to determine.

### The Interval

You would not see it arrive. You would notice that a crack in the ground had changed its mind.

On its planet, beneath an atmosphere dense enough to crush a submarine, the surface is a warm, translucent mineral. Pressure keeps it solid; heat keeps its internal structure restless. Mountains slowly rearrange without collapsing. Faults travel through the ground like weather.

The creature lives in those faults.

It is not made of a particular substance. It is a self-maintaining arrangement of imperfections: missing atoms, displaced crystal layers, and pockets of electrical strain. Matter passes into and out of its body without moving anywhere. As one region of mineral adopts the arrangement and another loses it, the creature travels.

A specimen might occupy a volume the size of a cathedral, although most of that volume is ordinary, unaltered rock. Its actual structure consists of thousands of disconnected, wafer-thin regions. What makes these regions one creature is their coordinated vibration.

Cut it in half and you might injure it. Remove the entire middle third and you might not.

### What it looks like

Under artificial light, an Interval resembles a collection of transparent surfaces that cannot quite agree about where they are.

Some bend light sharply. Others delay it. Seen through an inhabited patch of ground, your hand would appear in several positions at once—not because the creature creates illusions, but because light takes different amounts of time to cross different parts of its body.

Its edges are more visible than its interior: faint silver angles, abruptly truncated curves, a dark plane that vanishes when you lean closer. These features change when it exerts itself. During rapid movement, a brief violet flash passes through the mineral, followed several seconds later by a dry click.

There is no useful distinction between its inside and its outside. Small Intervals can pass through large ones. Sometimes both survive. Sometimes they exchange parts of their identities.

### How it lives

The planet’s moons flex its crust. The Interval feeds on the resulting strain.

It arranges its defects so that stressed mineral relaxes through a sequence of tiny transformations, capturing some of the released energy to maintain its own pattern. Behind it, the ground becomes clearer, colder, and slightly less able to carry sound.

An exhausted landscape is therefore not barren-looking. It is unnaturally quiet.

The creature cannot sense light. Its world consists of possible fractures.

A distant object is perceptible because it changes how pressure might travel through the ground. An approaching storm is a vast alteration in the range of available movements. Another Interval is recognizable by the stresses it chooses not to release.

It can detect a buried cavity hundreds of kilometres away yet remain unaware of a bright machine resting directly above it.

### Its experience of time

The Interval does not have a central brain. Information persists in standing vibrations distributed across its body.

Some parts complete a processing cycle in milliseconds. Others require years. Neither is subordinate to the other. A brief disturbance can provoke an immediate withdrawal while also entering a much slower process that will eventually change where the creature migrates.

It might still be deciding how to respond to an injury after the damaged region has regenerated.

Memory has physical consequences. An old Interval carries elaborate arrangements that no longer help it feed but preserve the effects of previous encounters. These make its movements inefficient and distinctive. Erasing them would make it healthier, faster—and no longer quite the same creature.

### Reproduction

To reproduce, two or more Intervals establish a shared vibration across a region none of them occupies.

They sustain it until the untouched mineral begins correcting disturbances on its own.

The offspring is not a miniature parent. It begins as a relationship among them, then gradually becomes independent. Its boundaries may overlap its parents’ bodies for centuries. During this period, a single remembered event can belong to several individuals, with no original owner.

There are no eggs, births, or first breaths. There is only a point after which the parents can fall silent and something continues answering.

### Meeting one

Your first conversation would probably be an accident.

A drilling machine would impose a repeated stress pattern. The Interval would alter the rock to return it. Engineers would compensate for the unexpected vibration. The creature would respond to that compensation.

Eventually, someone would shut the drill down.

Deep below, the Interval would continue preparing the next reply, patiently reshaping a kilometre of crystal around a silence it had not yet learned to interpret.

### The Unclosed

You would not notice it arriving. Nothing would approach you, and nothing would leave. Instead, a region of the planet that had previously been ordinary would begin behaving as though its parts had made an agreement.

It lives deep inside a planet with no solid surface, beneath thousands of kilometers of dense atmosphere and hot ocean. These tides bend the crystal, alter its conductivity, and generate electrical gradients. To the Unclosed, those changes provide nourishment, information, and the nearest equivalent its world has to weather.

#### What constitutes its body

The Unclosed is not made from a particular collection of atoms.

Its body is a self-maintaining arrangement of defects in the crystal: places where atomic rows fail to align, where electrical charges become trapped, and where neighboring regions conduct differently. These defects form an elaborate, shifting network several kilometers across.

The material continually passes out of its control. New material is recruited. What persists is the relationship between the defects.

At the center of this arrangement—although not necessarily at its geometric center—is an almost-complete circuit. The circuit must never quite close. If it closes, its stored energy discharges and the organization collapses into ordinary mineral imperfections.

Maintaining that tiny interruption requires the activity of the entire vast network.

It has no skin. Its boundary is the point beyond which it can no longer reliably correct a disturbance. When well supplied with energy, that boundary spreads. During difficult periods, whole regions become merely geology again.

#### What it would look like

To human eyes, it would be invisible within an opaque, incandescent substance.

But imagine an instrument that translates electrical strain into visible light. Through it, the Unclosed would appear as a volume of interrupted geometry: thin planes that nearly intersect, branching seams that stop just short of joining, dark intervals shifting among luminous sheets.

Nothing resembles a head or limb. There is no consistent direction in which it faces.

Its most conspicuous movements are absences. A bright plane develops a notch. The notch broadens, migrates, and disappears elsewhere. Several apparently disconnected structures change at once because they are parts of a single circuit extending outside your field of view.

A time-lapse would make it seem to fold without moving its material. Watched at human speed, it might appear motionless for days, then undergo a reorganization in less than a second.

#### How it lives

It feeds by channeling electrical currents through selected routes and using the resulting stresses to create, move, or erase crystal defects.

Uncontrolled current is dangerous. Too little allows its structure to deteriorate; too much heals the essential interruption by forcing a conductive path across it. Feeding is therefore a continuous act of precise refusal: it must take energy from its surroundings while denying that energy the easiest route.

Its waste consists of exhausted gradients and regions of unusually orderly crystal. An old individual leaves behind volumes of material so regular that they become difficult for another Unclosed to inhabit.

It does not travel by pushing itself through anything. It rearranges neighboring crystal into extensions of its organization, then relinquishes regions behind it. Crossing a kilometer might take a century. Under favorable conditions, it can instead remain in one place for millennia.

#### What it senses

It cannot distinguish objects by reflected light. It perceives how its surroundings might change.

A distant fracture alters the possible routes of electrical flow before the fracture reaches it. A moon’s approach changes the stresses that will become available. Another Unclosed modifies the local environment in ways that expose something of its internal organization.

Its sensory world is therefore composed of constraints: this route is becoming possible; that region will soon resist alteration; a disturbance here would propagate there.

Its memory is physical. Experiences leave defects that are costly to erase but easy to reactivate. An event from centuries earlier can shape its next response without ever becoming a representation of the past.

If it has awareness, an instant of that awareness may encompass several human years.

#### How it produces another

It does not make an egg, divide into equal portions, or construct a miniature copy.

Occasionally, it establishes a second essential gap within its network. For a time, the entire structure maintains both. Each region gradually develops the means to sustain its own interruption, while their shared connections become less necessary.

Eventually, a change in the planet’s tides makes those connections too expensive to preserve. They lapse.

There are now two creatures.

Neither is clearly the parent. Both inherit portions of the old organization, including memories that may be older than either of their independent existences. Sometimes they remain coupled for so long that whether there is one individual or two has no definite answer.

#### Its death

When the gap finally closes, there is no corpse.

A brief pulse of current passes through the surrounding crystal. Carefully maintained asymmetries relax. Some of the defects remain, but they no longer repair one another.

For a while, the region may still look almost exactly as it did when alive.

The difference is that the next disturbance goes unanswered.

It has no fixed size. In quiet conditions, it might occupy a region no larger than a cup. During a feeding event, the same individual could spread across several valleys.

Nor does it have a fixed number of pieces. Two distant patches can belong to one creature, while two interwoven patterns in the same slab of mineral can belong to different creatures.

What makes it one organism is that its parts continually correct one another’s behavior.

Istral’s crust never quite settles. Heat from above and below creates immense reserves of mechanical stress.

The Interval feeds by releasing that stress selectively.

It opens a microscopic vacancy at precisely the point where the surrounding crystal is about to rearrange. The rearrangement releases energy, part of which the creature captures as separated electrical charge. It spends that charge to create further vacancies elsewhere.

Uncontrolled, the process would become a fracture and exhaust itself. Alive, it advances through the rock as a carefully restrained possibility of breaking.

Its equivalent of starvation occurs in perfectly relaxed material. Its equivalent of burning occurs when the rock fractures too freely.

A feeding Interval is beautiful from the surface. Brief sheets of violet light flicker deep underground as charges discharge. The flashes trace no recognizable outline. You might watch for hours before realizing that the lights are not illuminating the creature; they are the waste products of its meals.

It does not distinguish objects by their surfaces. It distinguishes them by **how they would fail**.

A buried boulder is a particular family of possible fractures. A storm is a moving alteration in the weight and temperature of the ground. Another Interval is a region whose responses cannot be predicted without accounting for an independent set of decisions.

Its senses are active. It sends minute stress pulses through nearby minerals and reads the returning changes. To perceive something is to disturb it slightly.

It might spend days trying to determine what geological process you were.

Some remain within its active body. Others lie dormant across the landscape. When it encounters an old defect, the shape of that defect changes its behavior, restoring a previous response or association.

An ancient Interval therefore remembers partly by traveling.

Destroying a stretch of terrain can erase something it knows. Returning to a region abandoned centuries ago can restore a capacity it has not possessed since then.

Its identity is equally unfamiliar. Two individuals can overlap, exchange corrections, and gradually become one coordinated system. Later, that system may separate into three.

None is necessarily the parent, survivor, or copy.

At rare intervals, an individual constructs an elaborate arrangement of cavities in rock that contains almost no usable stress.

The work is expensive. It offers no obvious protection and attracts no mate.

Once completed, the creature sends a single pulse through it. The pulse passes among the cavities, dividing and returning in a pattern that can last for several days.

Then the Interval dismantles the structure.

Perhaps this is thought performed outside its body. Perhaps it is play.

From above, you would see only a faint shimmer under your boots—and then, very slowly, the shimmer changing its mind.

The planet’s tidal compression loads the crystal with energy. An ordinary fault releases that energy in a fracture. The Unfinished instead routes it through a controlled sequence of microscopic rearrangements.

The ground continues to carry its intricate pattern, sometimes for centuries. To another caesura, the place is unmistakably occupied—but nothing there can notice an arrival.

An adult occupies a region roughly two hundred meters across, although asking where it ends has no single answer. Some of its essential processes occur kilometers away.

Under artificial illumination, it resembles a set of transparent surfaces intersecting at angles that seem difficult to hold in your mind. These are not membranes. They are discontinuities in density and electrical behavior. Light passing through them splits into thin, offset images, so that an object behind the creature appears several times, each version distorted differently.

Its most conspicuous feature is a dark cavity that continually changes position.

The cavity is not inside the creature. It is a region the creature systematically excludes from its body. Maintaining that absence is essential to its survival: if mineral fluid within the cavity acquires the same organization as the surrounding surfaces, the entire organism collapses.

To human eyes, the Unbetween appears to spend its life carefully carrying a hole.

Vey’s interior slowly releases heat and electrical charge into its upper layers. The Unbetween survives by making that release happen along particular routes.

It holds some regions just below a phase transition and tips others across it. Each transition releases a little usable energy, which the creature spends restoring the delicate conditions elsewhere in its body. It is an elaborate, living cascade.

It does not eat objects. It consumes **opportunities for change**.

After it passes through a region, the material there looks almost untouched. But its gradients have been exhausted. For another Unbetween, that region is barren, even though every mineral and chemical ingredient remains present.

A starving individual becomes increasingly symmetrical. Its complex internal differences disappear until it is a beautiful, useless set of nested surfaces. Death is the moment its last asymmetry relaxes.

The Unbetween has no viewpoint.

The Unbetween approached. It reconstructed part of the probe’s thermal pattern within itself, altered it, and projected the altered pattern back through the fluid. The probe’s sensors recorded an intricate sequence of temperature changes lasting nineteen hours.
